Mr. Speaker, on June 3 the leader of the opposition moved a motion, and at the time the debate was adjourned I was making some remarks on it. It is now June 9, and as the motion was moved on June 3, for the benefit of those who may read Hansard today I think it would be in order if that motion were restated so that it would appear on today's record. As reported on page 2852 of Hansard for June 3, the motion reads as follows:
This house is of the opinion that the government should consider the advisability of taking steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth to seek means by which there may be convertibility of commonwealth currencies, and to explore all the possibilities for restoring and enlarging those traditional markets upon which our prosperity so largely depends.
At the time the debate was adjourned, I had made certain observations which I am not going to repeat. I have this to say to the leader of the opposition's motion, however, that it is one with which we do not disagree. In these days of force and dictatorship, we feel that any section of the public desirous of ironing out a difficulty around the conference table should have nothing put in its way to coming to an understanding on any problem; that is democracy at work. We have no objection to the motion on those grounds, but on the other hand I feel that the demand that the commonwealth countries alone should be consulted in a matter of international trade and the convertibility of currency is going into a field that is already established, and is narrowing down the possibility of reaching the solution to the international trade problem on a world-wide basis.
I believe we all recognize that after the last war international trade, as we understood it in the past, had been broken completely. There is no mechanism today whereby you can measure what international trade may be in the future. I believe that at the end of the war that was generally recognized, because all the allied nations involved in that war decided that international machinery would be necessary in order to iron out the world's problems. Everyone recognized that we were entering a new age, that we had reached the end of an era and that international trade, defence and related matters were matters that required the attention of an international body that would give each country the opportunity of getting around a conference table and deciding how these difficulties might be ironed out. It was then that the United Nations was formed.

All these social and economic problems were passed over to the United Nations. We have set up within the structure of the United Nations an organization known as the world food organization, for the purpose of ascertaining how the surpluses of the countries that have surpluses might be made available to the countries that were blasted out of production, and would therefore take a long time to return to a position whereby their resources might establish some reasonable standard of living for the people. In my opinion the proposal for a commonwealth conference on international trade and the convertibility of currency is, to a certain extent, entering the field that is already occupied by the United Nations. I should like the leader of the opposition, or any other member of his party who speaks later, to state what sort of machinery you are going to get at a conference between commonwealth nations that is not already available through the United Nations agency that is studying the problem.
It is suggested that we might have a commonwealth conference with Britain, Australia, New Zealand and Canada, nations that are already members of the world food organization, and who have the best brains available in their countries working in that organization to sell the idea of distribution of surpluses to the countries who have not the means with which to live.
In the second place, the problem is an economic one. Within the structure of the United Nations we have the economic organization, again with the experts from the various countries, advising as to ways and means of rehabilitating the economies of the backward countries. The problem of international trade and the distribution of goods is closely related to the economic problem. The convertibility of currencies, the stabilization of the currencies of the world, is another matter that the Bretton Woods conference ironed out. An international bank is established. The mechanics are there and in my opinion the United Nations is the organization to which we should be giving all the available information on the problems that are suggested for discussion by the motion of the leader of the opposition.
While I said that there is no harm in having a conference and an exchange of ideas, in the final analysis the solution, in my opinion, is not to be found within any bloc of nations. It is a world-wide problem. The world is so closely linked together that if we try to separate and to isolate any particular section of it, on the basis of economics or the distribution of food, then we are immediately getting into trouble.

I realize the fact that in the matter of defence it is necessary to set up regional pacts, as we have done. But again that regional pact is set up under the charter of the United Nations and is subject^ to examination from time to time by the United Nations. I do not like to see the suggestion, which is contained in the motion of the leader of the opposition, that we should isolate ourselves from the United Nations by the calling of a separate conference of the commonwealth nations to duplicate the responsibilities and authorities that we have centred in that world organization.
The second point that I should like to make is this. The leader of the opposition suggests a commonwealth conference. In his speech he presupposes that the centre of the problem is Great Britain herself. I agree with him that such is the case, but I do not think that any commonwealth conference, on the basis of international trade, is going to solve the problem of Britain. In my opinion, Britain's problem is one of population. Britain has 45 million to 50 million people centred in an area in which there are resources sufficient to maintain some kind of standard of living for perhaps 25 million or 30 million people. Again, I think that the question which Britain has to face up to and which the rest of the world must face up to is that of immigration.
I believe that the United Kingdom as such must consider the problem of relieving her economy by getting more of her people out to other parts of the commonwealth that are in a position to absorb them and where they can make some contribution. I think it is a backward way of doing things to keep Britain in the position in which she is, with the imports that she has to take in to feed her people and the exports that she has to send out in order to get the imports. She is in an impossible position with regard to arriving at any kind of solution to the problem of looking after her population, on the basis of the resources that she has at the present time.
My opinion is that Canada is in a position to absorb a large number of immigrants, properly selected and properly placed. To me it seems rather stupid for us on this continent to keep on producing and building up surpluses with the end in view of shipping those surpluses over to Britain, while at the same time the more we send over to Britain, the more she has to export in order to live. Instead of its being an economic problem that can be solved either by convertibility of her currency or by some international trade agreement, I think the crux of the problem is to be found in the population of Britain, based on the resources that she has at the present time.

Suggested Commonwealth Conference
It would have been different if the leader of the opposition had suggested that a conference of that kind should be called, for the purpose of determining Britain's future on the basis of population and available resources, with the end in view of zoning this country to tap the available resources all over this part of the North American continent in order to place immigrants there to develop new territories and new resources, and to create new wealth, to cut down the burden that Britain now has with regard to imports and exports on the basis of the population she has at the present time. That is quite a long story. It requires a great deal of analysis. I only mention it at this time because I think it is nearly time that we got around to considering that particular angle.
There is another thought that I should like to leave with members of the house before I sit down and it is this. With regard to many commodities in this country, we are neglecting our internal consuming market.
I am not going to go into the long story of beef and high prices. I have read a great deal on that subject within the last few months; and in my opinion we have lost in this country a terrific market for beef because of high prices. It is said: Put a floor under it. That is fine. But where you have a floor under something, you must have a ceiling; and there has not been a ceiling.
I believe that we have priced the average Canadian out of the beef market over the past year. I think that the government-the Department of Agriculture particularly- should take a look at that particular market because it is one in which at the present time we are getting pretty badly stuck. We have United States embargoes, and we have made a tripartite agreement with Great Britain and New Zealand to accept some of our surplus beef; but at the same time we have lost in this country, over the past couple of years, a large market right in Canada because we have fairly well priced ourselves out of the market. That situation applies not only to beef. I asked a question this afternoon as to why the price of potatoes in this country has doubled during the past month. What is the reason for that? In my opinion there is shortsightedness on somebody's part. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said he did not know why there was a shortage of potatoes. That is the responsibility of the Department of Agriculture. Is there a shortage of potatoes, or is it a matter of some smart persons in the centre, who have large warehouses in this country, storing potatoes and creating an 

artificial shortage so that they can get whatever price they want to put them on the market for? Remember the lesson of J. S. McLean with regard to butter. Butter was stored in this country and prices were driven up until they were sure that they had the market in the position where they could get the highest prices; that situation was not because of a shortage but because a shortage was deliberately created.
Our own market is the one that we should be regulating and watching carefully. In my opinion, if we watch it as carefully as we should, we may not be so dependent on export markets as we appear to be at the present time. There are a great many things that we can do within Canada to protect ourselves, in developing and maintaining our own internal consuming market; and that depends to a large extent on how we allow our prices to fluctuate in this country. With regard to a commodity which is as necessary as are potatoes to the average person's table, it is the responsibility of the government to see that a reasonable supply is available. There is no reason that I know of why, within the past six months, there should' be the terrific shortage of potatoes that there is supposed to be in Canada at the present time. It is no excuse to say that because a commodity is in short supply it should be that much more expensive. That is an illogical argument. It did not cost any more to produce those potatoes. They should not be any higher in price to the consuming public. It is merely a matter of someone who has control of the fixing of the price of the commodity taking the general public by the throat because of the fact there is a shortage. In my opinion there is now in the hands of the government machinery to stop that kind of thing through the resale price maintenance legislation under the Combines Investigation Act. I hope that that legislation is not just another statute that is put away to gather dust. I hope there is machinery behind that particular statute so that situations like the price of potatoes in the country today can be taken hold of and an investigation made and the general public not be hijacked as they appear to be at the present time.
How about when they were 25 cents a barrel?
Well, if the hon. member will tell me when they were 25 cents a barrel I will say something about it.
I can tell you they were 25 cents a barrel, on a number of occasions.
That is not information at all; it is just an assertion.
Well, you should know that.
I never paid 25 cents a barrel at any time I bought potatoes. I had to pay more than 25 cents a barrel.
That is all the farmers got.
I am not arguing the farmer's case at the present time; I am arguing the case of the consumer in Canada, and the question of markets and the relationship of the internal market to the export market.
I am not in agreement with the high prices at the present time.

We should start at home and put our own house in order. In any international relation I believe that the domestic economy should be the first yardstick. You cannot create chaos at home and expect to have an orderly market outside.
I made most of my remarks on this particular subject on June 3 when the amendment was moved by the leader of the opposition, and I am not going to extend them any further.

I regret that I was not in the house when the amendment was moved. I was unavoidably absent because I was taking part in the deliberations of a select committee; therefore I did not hear the speeches by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the greater part of the speech of the leader of the opposition. However, since that time I have read their speeches, and a number of other speeches that were made at that time. I was very disappointed that within those speeches I did not find any suggestion as to how the problems outlined in the amendment could be met.
However, before going on I should like to comment briefly on a few of the statements made by the previous speaker, with a number of which I agree. He referred to the fact that the United Nations Organization has a number of ancillary organizations that were attempting to deal with this problem. He referred to the food and agriculture organization. I agree with him that on that body there are some excellent men who have given a lot of study to the problem of getting surplus products to needy people in other countries. For instance, they introduced a proposal for a world food board. Then they also introduced a proposal to set up an international commodity clearing house, in my opinion both excellent proposals. But the member nations voted these proposals down, and in regard to the second of those, one of the main reasons it was turned down was that it violated the principles of the Bretton Woods agreement.
So far as the Bretton Woods agreement is concerned, as I will show later, there is no
9. 1952
Suggested Commonwealth Conference solution to this problem under that agreement. The hon. member also mentioned that we should expand consumption within Canada to help reduce some of our surpluses. With that I agree wholeheartedly. We have not developed the home market to anything like the extent to which it could be developed.
I also agree with him that we should help to solve the problems of over-congested countries such as Belgium and Britain by allowing greater immigration to this country. Having got these people over here, then of course it would be our responsibility to see that they do their share to help produce the wealth of the country and to see that the purchasing power of those people, along with the rest of Canada, is maintained at a level sufficiently high to buy the production of the country and the imports that are brought in, in exchange for our exports.
I am not going to quote the amendment because the hon. member has put it on the record; but the main problem dealt with in that amendment is the one of trying to get a market for our surplus production and providing ways and means by which that production can be paid for by the nations receiving it. I noted in the speeches made the other day repeated reference to the fact that Britain lacked dollars with which to buy the produce of the dollar areas. Well, the next conclusion arrived at is that the solution to that problem is to make sterling convertible into dollars. In that regard we have to remember that dollars do not originate within the sterling area; they originate within the dollar area, and the only way the sterling area can make sterling balances convertible into dollars would be by the dollar area providing those dollars to the sterling area by a number of methods; either by buying sufficient quantities of goods from the sterling area so that the sterling area would then be able to pay for the exports from this country, or by foreign investment within the sterling area. That would be especially worth while where the productivity of any country is low. Foreign investment would then be justified to the extent needed to increase that country's productivity, so that they would have more goods available with which to pay for imports.
In that regard let us not forget that if we indulge in that kind of program we will have to be prepared to accept imports resulting from that increased production; and it is doubtful whether we would be willing to do that, because we have not even today accepted all the exports that these nations are willing to send to this country. I am very doubtful whether, if we indulged in a

The other alternative of course is to make loans or gifts. I am not advocating either of those, because neither of those two things is a solution; they are merely a palliative. As I have pointed out, the solution to that problem of converting sterling into dollars must, to a very large extent, rest with the dollar area because dollars originate in dollar areas. For that reason I take direct issue with the Minister of Finance when he suggests that this is primarily a problem to be solved by the sterling area. The sterling area can never solve that problem unless the dollar area is prepared to make its dollars available to them in one way or another.
The Minister of Finance, with a certain amount of pride, referred to the fact that we have made the Canadian dollar convertible for the past few months, practically a year. But why is the Canadian dollar convertible into United States dollars today? It is convertible largely as a result of the action by the United States of America in making large-scale investments in this country, thereby providing us with dollars not only to balance our unfavourable balance of trade with the United States, but also to build up our reserves of gold and United States dollars. If the United States of America had not indulged in that large-scale program of foreign investment in this country we would not have the Canadian dollar convertible today, and we would not have the Canadian dollar at par with the United States dollar. It is largely the result of that fact that the Canadian dollar is being bolstered at the present time by the United States dollar.
In so far as the calling of a conference is concerned, I would support that idea, but I am afraid it would be just like former conferences; it would meet, and there would be very little result therefrom unless we are prepared to send men to that conference with power to tread new paths. If these men are going to be tied down to follow out policies as enunciated in the Bretton Woods agreement, they might just as well stay at home, because there is no solution under the Bretton Woods agreement.
It will be recalled that in 1945, when we were discussing the Bretton Woods agreement, I bitterly attacked it on the ground that it had a pro creditor bias. It gave credit nations the right to demand payment for their exports in their own currency without putting any responsibility upon them to accept imports in return, because the only way these nations accepting goods from us can pay for them


is by selling us goods in return in order to obtain our currency. If we refuse to balance trade with these nations, then it is impossible for them to pay us with dollars. I indicated at that time that these exporting nations should be prepared to accept the currency of the importing nations, and I shall have something to say on that later on.
The leader of the opposition stressed the fact that if war developed tomorrow, in all probability we would, overnight, find ways and means of getting our production to the area of the war-to Europe, if the war happened to be there. I would agree with him one hundred per cent, because that has always been the history. We have had difficulty in peacetime, but just as soon as war has been declared, the canons of sound finance have been silenced by the cannons of war.
What happened in the last war? Within a very short time the dollar sign was abolished. That, in fact, was the expression used by President Roosevelt. A cabinet minister in England said that the humbug of finance was done away with. A system of lend-lease was introduced which merely meant that the countries of Europe were allowed to pay for their imports by their exports. That is, it was understood that at a later date they would be in a position to export goods to us in payment for goods they received from us. The dollar sign was abolished.
Unfortunately, however, just as soon as the last cannon had been fired, those canons of sound finance once again began to function in this country. They did not even wait until the end of the war. They started sniping a year before the war was over, because it was in 1944 the Bretton Woods agreement originated. If lend-lease had continued after the war, I am satisfied we would not be facing the difficulties we are facing today. I quite agree that lend-lease would have had to be modified in many ways, and I shall deal with some of the modifications I think should have been made to the lend-lease program in order to make it an effective instrument by which goods and services could be got to those countries needing them.
The present situation is a serious one. The sterling area is facing one of the worst crises in its history. In the last year its reserve of dollars and gold has gone down by over two-thirds. The leader of the opposition also referred to the fact that in the past multilateral trade and convertibility had worked fairly satisfactorily and apparently he felt that in view of the fact it had worked in the past there is no reason why it should not work in the future.

I think the reason is shown pretty clearly by a statement made by a former deputy minister, Mr. M. W. Mackenzie, on October 9, 1947. This statement, appearing in Foreign Trade, is important, because it deals with this very subject:
Our commodity exports to the United States have never been as great as our imports from that country, and even in prewar years the difference used to be of the order of one or two hundred millions. In the year 1929 it reached a prewar peak of $400 million. It was possible for this situation to develop because there was a lengthy period in which a well-working system of multilateral payments made it unnecessary for Canada, or for any other country, to be greatly concerned with its bilateral trade balances. The free convertibility of currencies provided us with a ready means of squaring our accounts with all countries, regardless of the size of the balance in any one direction. Now that the multilateral system of payments has suffered a serious breakdown for the second time, or perhaps one should say for the third time in the last generation, Canada and all other countries that are engaged heavily in international trade are facing a difficult stage in their affairs. The balance of trade between pairs of countries-that is, a bilateral balance-has become a matter of first importance and will remain so until the mechanism of the multilateral system has once more been placed in good order. That in itself is a tremendous and complex task, requiring measures of many different kinds. It is a job that will require time, even under the best of circumstances.
I think one should remember that since that time, when multilateral trade was working fairly well, and it was possible to have convertibility of currency, a great change has taken place in regard to the sterling area. Great Britain has lost a very large percentage of her foreign investments, investments which gave her access to American dollars. She also expanded her external debt very considerably, which means that a large amount of her exports today are unrequited.
I hold in my hand a document entitled "Survey '52; Where We Stand This Year". This purports to be an official account in popular form of the economic situation and prospects for 1952. It is published by the British government. In part, it says:
The present crisis is the worst yet. Between June, 1951, and March, 1952, nearly two-thirds of the gold and dollar reserves vanished.
Then it goes on to say:
In the meantime our own position had greatly worsened, too. On the one hand the import bill was leaping upwards: we were rebuilding our stocks, which had been heavily run down in 1950. On the other hand, exports were limited. They were limited in three ways: by the growing pressure of rearmament on the metal goods industries; by the shortage of steel which hampered the further growth in production; and by the falling overseas demand for consumer goods. So they rose scarcely at all. On top of that, there were the loss of Persian oil and the commencement of payments on the North American loans.

So it seems an odd time, really, to suggest that we should try to bring about the convertibility of sterling and American dollars.
Where did the statement come from?

It is an official account in popular form of the economic situation and prospects for 1952, and purports to have been prepared for Her Majesty's government by the information division of the treasury and the central office of information. I received it by mail, and thought perhaps all hon. members had received it.
I believe any time a person criticizes government policy or government proposals he should be prepared to make some constructive proposals in regard to ways and means by which that problem can be met. I have certain suggestions to make. Perhaps I should admit at once that these are not original; they were not my idea, but rather ideas I picked up. Perhaps I should mention where I got them, in the first place.
I was in England in 1938, and on that occasion met the late Lord Bennett and had with him a long and interesting discussion on the question of international trade, especially as it affected Canada. He suggested to me that I should meet the secretary of the London Chamber of Commerce, Mr. A. de V. Leigh, and introduced me to him. I had a most interesting talk with Mr. Leigh who, I consider, is a man at the top in his business. We know that the London Chamber of Commerce has perhaps had more experience on questions of international trade than any other body in the world. They are not just a bunch of pseudo-economists; they are men who have been engaged in business and in international trade for generations. Those men know what they are talking about.
When I came back to Canada I was particularly interested a couple of years later to receive from Mr. Leigh a copy of the report of the London Chamber of Commerce in which it deals with the general principles of a post-war economy. I should like to read one paragraph from that report:
The chamber, having considered whether there is any system which would achieve, wholly or partially, the solution of all the above problems, generally accepts the principles laid down in "A Twentieth Century Economic System," especially in respect of blocked credits for the payment of international obligations.
And then a footnote says that the publication "A Twentieth Century Economic System" is obtainable from the Economic Reform Club. It is interesting to note that "A Twentieth Century Economic System" is a little book

Suggested Commonwealth Conference whose author does not give his name. I quote from the front page where it says:
The author has decided to remain anonymous, in the hope that his fellow citizens will insist, on this occasion, on doing their own thinking, and will consider these proposals on their merits, uninfluenced by the names and reputations of the protagonists on either side.
I know the names of the men who were connected with that, but I do not feel free to mention those names in view of the fact that, apparently, they desire to remain anonymous. But they are men who have had a great deal of experience in regard to the question of international trade. I want to deal briefly with some of the proposals contained in the "twentieth century system". First of all it advocates that all exporting nations shall accept the currency of the importing nation. It points out that after all the main purpose of trade is the exchange of goods and services, and when you sell goods to another nation on that basis then all you require is a currency that will permit you to buy other goods and services from that country. If we export goods to Great Britain we do not need dollars in order to buy British goods. All we need is sterling with which we can buy goods or services from Great Britain.
Therefore it lays down a principle which is just the opposite of the principle enunciated under the Bretton Woods agreement. It lays down the principle that the exporting nation must accept the currency of the importing nation instead of having the right to demand payment in its own currency which forces the importing country into an unpayable debt unless the exporting nation is prepared to buy an equivalent amount of imports from that country. That is the first principle that it lays down. It also advocates that the rate of exchange should be mutually agreed upon, and it also states that a steady price level should be maintained with respect to export trade between those nations.
The method of doing business would be quite a simple one. It would provide for convertibility but convertibility by the exporting country. In other words, the dollar area would convert bills in sterling to dollars and the sterling area would convert bills in dollars into sterling. Let us take, for instance, a Canadian exporter who draws a bill in sterling on a British firm. The Canadian firm would merely take the bill drawn in sterling to the chartered banks, discount it and receive dollars. The chartered bank would turn it over to the foreign exchange control board. In view of the fact that we have no such body now he would turn it over to the Bank of Canada.
[Mr. Qyelch.l
In England the importer upon presentation of the bill would pay in sterling to their commercial banks and that sterling would be turned over to the Bank of England. Then the Bank of Canada would have a balance of sterling within the Bank of England and vice versa. When a British exporter exported goods to Canada exactly the same procedure would be adopted. Therefore in return for our exports we would have a sterling balance in England and the British in return for their exports to Canada would have a dollar balance in the Bank of Canada. As long as we balanced our trade no further action would be required. The only thing we could use our sterling balance in Great Britain for would be to buy goods and services within that country. That would be in order to carry out legitimate trade. If we refused to buy, the balance would remain there and we would get nothing for it. There would be no question of debt. There would be no interest drawn upon it and it would not cause any embarrassment to the sterling area.
So far as our exporters are concerned, they would be happy because they would be receiving dollars, and so far as the British exporters are concerned they would be quite happy because they would be paid in their own currency. If for any reason we did not wish to bring in more imports we would of course have the alternative of investing our sterling balance in England in some enterprise to help expand the production of that country. The situation might be that Great Britain actually did not have sufficient exports to meet our requirements. Then we would be quite justified in using some of that sterling balance for the purpose of developing resources in the sterling area.
Before anybody attacks that idea let me remind them that that is exactly what the United States has done with regard to Canada. For years Canada has had a great deal of difficulty in balancing her trade with the United States. This year we had an unfavourable balance of trade with the United States of over $900 million, and with the world at large of $500 million. The only reason we were able to meet that unfavourable balance of trade was because the United States made large investments in this country which made it possible for us not only to meet our unfavourable balance of trade but also to develop our resources. That was the result of the United States investing money in this country. It might also be a healthy situation for us to make investments abroad so that the returns from those investments would help to offset the money that we have to pay

to the citizens of the United States on their investments in this country. One would help to balance the other.
The question of the United States policy of investing money in Canada is a debatable one. By that I mean it is debatable whether or not it is really beneficial to Canada. There is no doubt that much of their investment has been a great help to Canada. It has helped us to build up our oil industry. It has helped us to develop iron ore and various other things, but a great deal of their investment has been of another nature. A large amount of United States investment has been for the purchase of dominion and provincial bonds and securities, and that is not quite such a healthy picture. Therefore when Canadians are apt to be a little bit boastful about the Canadian dollar being above par it seems to me they should remember that the only reason it is above par today is because it is actually being bolstered by the United States. No one can say it is a very healthy situation when a country, in order to meet its unfavourable balance of trade that is a deficit on current account, has to turn over a certain amount of its capital in order to achieve that balance, and that is exactly what has happened in so far as Canada and the United States are concerned. It is rather interesting to note the viewpoint of a United States citizen on this subject. I have here an extract from the Calgary Herald of March 26, 1952. It is an article by John Harriman of the North American newspaper alliance. The heading of the article is, "Americans control quarter of Canada's manufacturing. Capital still flowing in." The article reads as follows:
Is American business going to take over Canadian industry? If Canadians are not worried about this, they should be, for we have been pouring capital into their country at an unprecedented rate and buying both properties and securities right and left. There are now 2,500 United States firms in Canada. And these United States firms account for a total of 25 per cent of all Canadian manufactures. In the last two years about $2 billion in United States capital has flowed northward to finance the current Canadian boom, bringing our investment in that country today to an unprecedented $8 billion, which is about 70 per cent of all United States investment abroad. Last year Americans bought heavily of Canadian corporate securities-about $400 million. Back in the summer of 1950, United States investors bought $195 million of Canadian government bonds, which so bolstered the currency of that country that the Canadian dollar was unpegged from the rate of 90 cents to the United States dollar.
In the light of that I do not really think there is anything for Canadians to boast about. As I say, it has happened as a result of action originating in the United States. With respect to the sterling area, the countries in that area have a great deal of difficulty in

It is a situation very similar to that which exists between the United States and Canada. The Minister of Finance says that it is for Great Britain to deal with it. I say that in exactly the same way that the United States has helped us in this situation we should be prepared to do likewise with regard to the sterling area. I think at this time a certain amount of investment in the sterling area, for the purpose of building up some of their backward industries and increasing their efficiency so as to make it possible for them to export more of the type of goods that we want, would be well worth while.
Once that has been accomplished we will have to be prepared to accept those imports to a far greater degree than we have in the past. If we are going to be prepared to accept imports in future from the sterling area, then I think we will have to be very careful to see that at all times we maintain the purchasing power of the people of Canada at a sufficiently high level to buy those goods. Nobody can convince me that there are not hundreds of thousands of people in Canada who would be only too pleased to receive much of the goods that we could bring in from Great Britain today. The reason they are not buying is not because they do not want them but because their income does not permit. Therefore, in trying to solve this international problem, there is also a national problem to be solved at the same time. The first step is to maintain the purchasing power of your own people at a level which makes it possible for them to purchase the goods brought in in exchange for our exports. The second point is to provide a means by which other nations can purchase our exports.
In closing I would say I am prepared to support this amendment because I believe a conference could accomplish a great deal in bringing about a greater amount of trade between this country and the sterling area- provided we sent to that conference men who are prepared and allowed to tread new paths.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to trespass at any great length on the time of the house, but there are one or two things that might be said and that have not been dealt with in detail as yet.
I think it is particularly fitting that we should on this day be discussing this resolution; that we should on this occasion of the

Suggested Commonwealth Conference queen's birthday be dealing with the advisability of taking steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth to seek means by which there may be convertibility of commonwealth currency, and to explore the possibilities of restoring and enlarging those traditional markets upon which our prosperity so largely depends.
As I listened this afternoon to the united singing on the part of all members of this house of the anthem that is national to every part of this British commonwealth, I thought of the words of John Masefield, poet laureate, which I feel express the attitude of consecration of all of us to the concept of the crown: An order and a beauty from of old,
Set by its virtue above greed and hate:
A loneliness of living crowned with gold,
In all life's storm, a standard of the state.
I think in those words are epitomized the attitude and concept of peoples everywhere within the British commonwealth.
I am sure the house listened with interest and attention to the address of the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) who has just concluded, and in particular when he dealt with the situation whereby we in this country, as the years go by, are becoming more and more a magnetic attraction for investment by people from the United States, and less and less on the part of Britain. Britain had large investments in Canada prior to the first great war. I speak from recollection, but my memory is that they amounted to some $4 billion. Today, to all intents and purposes, they are largely dissipated because Britain found, as a result of the need for preservation of freedom, that all her resources should be liquidated and disposed of in the interests of our common survival.
Some two years ago-on February 28, 1950-I moved a resolution in this house, seconded by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), in connection with this very matter. That resolution was:
This house is of the opinion that the government should take immediate steps to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of the nations of the British commonwealth and] countries of the empire to devise policies to restore our lost markets and thereby to provide jobs for our Canadian people.

I would like to point out that, in connection with agriculture, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, on March 6, dealt with that very point in its representations to the cabinet. They said as follows:
We regret that after six years, F.A.O. has not succeeded in establishing a practical international commodity program. To take the position that Canada and other advanced countries should produce to capacity because people somewhere need the product is a fine humanitarian point of view, but it is a theoretical and impractical one unless an international commodity program exists to organize and supervise distribution.
The world is waiting for leadership from governments in F.A.O. to establish a commodity program which would undertake the three-fold function of meeting emergency shortages and famine, of holding reserve stocks and of managing surpluses.
We were pleased to see that our government representatives at the last F.A.O. conference supported the view that some kind of international food board would be necessary if the world were to embark realistically on a policy of unlimited production of food for the world's needy people. We urge the government to continue its support . . .
... in this direction.
The FAO has not succeeded, and we Canadians find ourselves in the position that the Conservative party said as far back as February, 1950, would result unless action was taken. At that time we warned of the danger first of accumulating surpluses of agricultural products, and secondly of the fact that we had no available machinery to provide for distribution and therefore to assure prosperity not only for agriculture but

for our people as a whole. We contended that markets were being lost. However, the attitude of the government at that time was that markets for agricultural products were being provided in the United States of America. Certainly the United States market is close at hand, contiguous, and easily available, but experience has shown that when surpluses pile up in agricultural products those surpluses are as common to the United States as they are to Canada. At such times that market is a most tenuous one and difficult to maintain.
We are now faced with the loss of our market for beef on another ground, and we hope the loss of that market will be temporary. It is to be hoped that the expressed belief that by September the United States market will be made available to Canadian beef will prove to be a fact. We have learned in the last two years that the British market is, after all, the best market for Canadian agricultural products. Statements to that effect were made when we spoke in 1950. It is the most certain market, and it does not depend upon the changing conditions of the United States. We have lost our markets in Britain. In his address the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) indicated that the markets have not been lost, but that we are out of the market by reason of our own actions.
We were promised farm markets. Some years ago the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) pointed out that one of the reasons that the western provinces were required to sell wheat at less than world prices was che fact that by so doing markets were provided for other farm products. -our trade with the United Kingdom is of vital importance to us. Indeed, such commerce is part of the geographical pattern of the North Atlantic area, as witness Newfoundland, which has been the extreme example of the close economic ties between British North America and Great Britain. It is therefore important to remember that we have historic and economic ties which also run on an east-west line. The St. Lawrence river and the Laurentian shield have profoundly affected our economy since the beginning and will continue to do so. The boundary between Canada and the United States is for the most part no arbitrary line but responds to certain economic realities which would have asserted themselves even if North America had been a political unit. Hence the development of our trade with Europe to which, indeed, we are geographically closer than is the United States.
Then also from the same book, "On Being Canadian", I think these are extremely pertinent thoughts at this date:
There are good reasons why the commonwealth is of importance to us in our national life; important both in our relations abroad and in our domestic affairs. For one thing, we have greater influence in the world as a member of the British family than would otherwise be ours. Membership gives us in a sense a double status. It provides one of the rare instances in which one can "eat one's cake and have it too". I feel sure from my own experience that the fact that Canada appears on the international scene, not only as an important country on her own account, but also as a member of a great world association, lends her enhanced prestige. In the international world, prestige means influence.
As far as domestic affairs are concerned, there is a persistent illusion in the minds of some people that the British connection has somehow a limiting effect on our national growth; that the term "dominion" is derogatory to our national dignity. "Dominion" is only a word, and it has all but disappeared. In any event, it is important to consider things rather than their labels. In Canada we have certain institutions and traditions and characteristics which give us, whatever language we speak, our meaning as a separate country. Without the British connection these things would steadily evaporate and we should) have less and less significance as an individual state. How long would a Canadian republic maintain its individuality here in North America? The forms of our sovereignty might be retained, but we should be caught inexorably by the southward undertow and completely assimilated to American life.
The words of that great work which I have quoted must give to us a realization that there is something worth while to preserve; that with Britain in the position in which she finds herself, we should be doing something to uphold and to maintain her spirit for she stands today, as in the past, as the bulwark of freedom.
The first suggestion is the one embodied in the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition, namely, the need to convene a British commonwealth trade conference. Some say that it will have no results. There can be no harm in trying. Certainly our markets are disappearing. Certainly the

Suggested Commonwealth Conference problems of convertibility are great. But whether they are great or not, surely they are not overwhelming. Bringing together at this time such a conference, in mobilizing the hopes of peoples everywhere within this commonwealth, would have an effect which could not be obtained in any other way. Certainly there could not but be effective results from these representative statesmen of the commonwealth meeting together to discuss the problems of what can be done to maintain these markets, to extend our trade channels, to consider the question of convertibility and also the possibility of Canada's purchasing within the sterling bloc raw materials now secured elsewhere; it would be a conference similar to that which has been suggested on several occasions by the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon).
Britain finds herself in a position of trading with communist countries in order to secure metal, grain and lumber in return for machinery, rubber and precision tools, or has during the past year; that trade is now being reduced. Certainly we will get no results by doing nothing. However certain that some are that such a conference would not succeed, nevertheless I believe that it would be a message of hope to every part of this commonwealth and would be as well the expression at least of a hope that the farmers, who today in our country face a situation that is dangerous to the national economy, would at least have every avenue for trade explored.
Secondly, I suggest to the Minister of Defence Production, who has a vast knowledge of the subject, that every ordinary person like myself realizes that Britain is in a position where she has not available Canadian funds to make purchases of Canadian products. Is it beyond the capacity of Canadian and British statesmen to arrive at an agreement under which the minister could divert to Britain $90 million to $100 million of Canadian defence needs that are today being purchased in the United States, thereby assuring that the moneys made available in consequence of that diversion would be utilized for the purchase of farm surpluses that are piling up today? Mr. Speaker, they are piling up. If you put pork in cans, it still becomes a surplus that piles up. We have purchased some 30 million pounds of surplus pork at a price of between $18 million and $19 million. We can put that in cans but it is still surplus and it has to be disposed of.
I believe that in a British commonwealth resources and development trade conference there is a hope that fat least something will be done to untangle the snarls in traffic
3040	HOUSE OF
Suggested Commonwealth Conference which are causing fears for the future to be expressed, and with reason, by farmers and by other producers within our country.
Thirdly, and this is a personal suggestion, Britain finds herself in the position where her people are living on a food level far below anything that we in this country have ever undergone. Surpluses in our country are piling up. In the days prior to the last war surpluses in various parts of the world were disiposed of by destruction. Coffee, cotton, sugar and hogs were destroyed in order to reduce the glut of production. Surpluses are being piled up in our own country; and by next fall the situation may well be much more serious than it is now.
Can we afford, sir, in a world in which statesmen contend, and as the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) has said on many occasions, that the raising of standards of living is one of the means to withstand the onrush of communism, to neglect to do our duty by giving assistance? We are making our contribution to the Colombo plan. Would it be beyond what is fair to consider a grant from the people of Canada of a food gift to Britain in order, first, to assist that country, and secondly, to remove the effect of an overhanging deluge of a surplus that will inevitably occur unless something is done?
I know that there are some who say that this cannot be done. That argument does not apply to a British commonwealth conference. If it is not successful we in Canada would have at least discharged our responsibility. The situation is serious in Britain. One cannot say that that is their domestic issue alone, because after all we in co-operation with the United States either stand or fall together for freedom should freedom ever be challenged. When one reads the newspaper headlines today one cannot but realize the situation that exists in Berlin is a dangerous one. I believe that the U.S.S.R. cannot continue forever to talk tough without action; yet one can but hope that that situation will not turn out dangerously to world peace. Britain needs something of an uplift that such a gift would give her.
Somebody may argue that it would prove costly. All I can say is that the beef deal that has been made as a result of the exchange of opinions between New Zealand, the United States, Britain and Canada may also prove costly. The pork packing plan to dispose of pork in cans may also prove costly. The fear of an overhanging surplus on prices will always prove costly, because, unless something is done to remove that surplus, the loss will finally rest upon the Canadian


people. For that reason I ask for consideration by the Canadian government even yet of a free vote in this house on the question as to whether or not there should be a British commonwealth trade conference. Certainly in 1950, when the resolution was moved in this house, my party was not astray in the expression of our point of view. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) seconded the resolution and spoke on it. He pointed out the dangers of a loss of the markets for agricultural products. What was said then has unfortunately proved too true. It is not for us to speculate on what would have happened had that resolution been accepted two years ago. But one thing we do know, namely that things would not be as bad as they are today in so far as the prospects of Canadian agriculture are concerned.
Somebody will say that the amendment amounts to a vote of non-confidence. I think of cases having the same effect that have come before this house, yet the government has released its membership from so considering it. I think of the milk subsidy discussion. There was an occasion when parliament was free to vote.
The situation is anything but hopeful, Mr. Speaker, in so far as agriculture is concerned. It is not hopeless. There is a step that we can take, and that is by calling together a commonwealth conference. When there are problems that are difficult of solution in the international sphere, our ministers go all over the world. They are the most ambulant and circumambulant ministry we have ever had. When international affairs are at stake they believe in conferences; they believe in putting their feet under the table with other nations. Cannot we afford to adopt a similar attitude among our own kith and kin within the British commonwealth and endeavour, in co-operation with the United States, to arrive at something which will remove the overhanging fear that today haunts the farmers of this country-the fear that in the failure to act we sacrifice the possibility of preserving our agriculture industry intact, in the light of our responsibilities and the opportunities we have to act now?

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that before I deal in a detailed way with the motion before the house and the amendment of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), perhaps I should spend a moment or two of my time in dealing with the speech of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) who has immediately preceded me in the debate.

I would refer first to his statement that the amendment is not a want of confidence motion. I do not know just how he arrives at that conclusion because, as I understand it, a want of confidence vote is a vote upon any material and major matter of government policy. As I heard the speeches of members of the official opposition, last Tuesday and again today, I understood them to address most of their remarks to international trade. My understanding of international trade is that its significance, as expressed in terms of fractions, is that it involves about one quarter to one third of all our national income. It is a tremendous factor affecting this country. Perhaps it is more important to us than to any other country in the world.
For the hon. member for Lake Centre to assert in the House of Commons that a vote on a motion dealing with international trade is not a want of confidence motion, just is not tenable. I cannot see how the amendment can be considered as other than a vote of want of confidence in the government.
Then, there are one or two other observations he made which, it seems to me, require attention. He said he was going to set out in detail the markets we have lost. That, of course, is his privilege. Then he used some figures in support of his contention. First of all, he picked out only certain products, certain items. I am not criticizing him for that because, obviously, it would be impossible to go over all of them. But I do think it is desirable that we understand that that was done.
It will be seen at once that in picking out particular items of our export trade with the United Kingdom he was dealing with items they are not importing, presumably because of their dollar shortage. Then necessarily he becomes involved in going a step further and deciding that we would choose which products are to be exported to the United Kingdom, and that they would have no more say about it.
For instance, he suggests they would no longer have the right to choose the cheaper product, or the product which would go farther in feeding a larger number of people. I am sure the hon. member did not wish to assert that proposition. Yet that is the only conclusion to be drawn from his remarks, if one is to be logical in analysing them.
Then he used the general expression, "They tell a story." Of course they tell a story. I presume that is what the hon. member was trying to do; and I would have thought that in telling the story he would
Suggested Commonwealth Conference have explained that in 1945, one of the years he mentioned, there was a war on, and the traditional suppliers of many of the products with which he dealt had been overrun by the enemy, with the result that those products could not go to the United Kingdom from that area. I refer specifically to countries such as Denmark and Holland. I should have thought that some other figures could have been chosen to illustrate his point.
They tell another story. He could have placed before the house the trade statistics for the years 1938, 1951 and 1952 showing exports to the United Kingdom. Those figures would have shown that, in the field of agricultural and vegetable products, in 1938 we exported to that country those goods to a value of $3,737,000, while in 1951 the figure had risen to $13,279,000 and in 1952 to $22,857,000.
All the observations by members of the official opposition about changes in dollar value cannot explain away an increase, six or seven times over, in the amount of agricultural and vegetable products going from Canada to the United Kingdom in 1952 as compared with 1938. And of course in using those figures I must be quick to point out that the United Kingdom buys more grains now, and less of certain animal products. Their reason for doing this is perfectly simple and obvious. Those grains will feed more people for less money. It is a matter of common knowledge in the world of trade, and in the general field of health and nutrition, that it is cheaper to feed people with grain products than with animals and animal products.
Returning now to the matter before the house, I would point out that the amendment of the leader of the opposition is in language that indicates that he wants this government to convene at the earliest possible date a conference of British commonwealth nations to seek means by which there may be convertibility, and then to go on to explore the possibilities for increasing trade and enlarging traditional markets.
It will be seen at a glance that the essential part of the amendment is that the Canadian government is to convene the meeting, that it is further tied down by the fact that it must be done at the earliest possible time, and that the most important matter to be discussed is that of convertibility.
Notwithstanding the fact that these are the points set out in the amendment offered by the official opposition, practically all their discussion has been about trade matters. I should point out that hon. members in other opposition groups did not make that mistake,

The facts are that at the start of the accelerated defence preparedness program an attempt was made to buy machine tools from the United Kingdom. However, orders only to the extent of some $6 million were placed in that country. The facts are quite simple as to that situation. Their equipment is highly competitive and is good. Their prices are highly competitive. I think they are probably cheaper than elsewhere. The difficulty is simply that the United Kingdom was not able to supply that equipment, and it is no fault of theirs that they were not able to do so. They must assume responsibility for the management of their own affairs internally, and they had losses arising out of the war and restoration work in their own country because of war damage. They must now allocate some of their own productive effort, in a quantity to be determined by themselves, to defence preparedness in common with the other freedom loving countries of the world. The necessary climate for the convertibility of currency is very similar to the necessary climate for international trade. Currency convertibility requires three basic conditions. The first condition is that internal fiscal stability shall be maintained as a national policy. In other words there must be no resort to the issuing of money not represented by goods; the printing press must not be used. Inflation must be curbed in every possible way. There must be a balanced budget. If this factor is not present, no country whose internal fiscal policy is not sound can maintain a currency which will stand free convertibility. No matter what other conditions may exist, unless the internal fiscal policy is sound the national currency will not be sound.
The second condition is the removal by governments of artificial barriers to trade such as quotas, embargoes and all the devilish devices generally classified as exchange controls. Included in that are also government trading agencies. Never has international trade been carried on prosperously with a government as one of the parties to a deal. It may be urged that what, any other country does is none of our business. It may be said that we are offering advice to others if we mention these things. But, Mr. Speaker, these are inevitable and essential economic truths; and unless these conditions pertain there can be no really free and adequate convertibility of currencies. You cannot have a free currency or a freely exchanged currency unless a government will allow that currency to move in or out and be exchanged. At the present time those of us on the North American continent are in possibly the only
area in the world where there is a degree 
and it is not in any way complete-of free currency exchangeability. That is the second condition which must be present in order to make a currency convertible.

In other words the internal fiscal policy in the United States constantly reduces the purchasing price of the American national currency. There was an example this very week in connection with the negotiations regarding the steel strike, in which was involved an increase in the basic wage by something more than 20 cents. This will inevitably mean an increase in the price of basic steel. An increase in the price of basic steel inevitably means a depreciated purchasing power for the national currency. It cannot mean anything else. Therefore our adherence to this policy of using the United States dollar as an exchange medium is one of the greatest fallacies we could follow.

If your plant reduces capacity by as little as 10 per cent, your tax revenue may drop off as much as 40 per cent, because it is on 100 per cent operation that the profits are made. If, as we must expect, production falls off from the peak even by a small amount, the profits fall off by a large amount and the revenue for government purposes falls off by that corresponding amount. If we do not produce at 100 per cent of capacity our tax revenues will fall off. With such a large increment of taxes from one source, we stand in grave danger of having an unbalanced budget.

speakeroldname: Hon. Lionel Chevrier (Minister of Transport) moved
subtopic: PROVISION TO RELEASE CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS FROM CERTAIN CLAIMS BY HER MAJESTY IN EXCHANGE FOR PREFERRED STOCK, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 308, to revise the capital structure of the Canadian National Railway Company and to provide for certain other financial matters.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in the debate on the resolution preceding the introduction of this bill I made some general remarks on the principle outlined in the resolution. I shall now review in more detail the provisions of the bill. The Canadian National Railway system is made up of four principal railways. The Canadian National Railway Company has absorbed by amalgamation the old Grand Trunk system. It controls by stock ownership the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk Pacific systems. The Canadian National Railway Company has also been entrusted with the management and operation of the Canadian government railways which include the Intercolonial Railway, the National Transcontinental Railway, the Newfoundland Railway and the Hudson Bay Railway.
These four principal railways including their subsidiaries are generally referred to under the collective name of Canadian National Railways. Operations as a unified system commenced on January 1, 1923 and have continued under different forms of management to the present day. At the present time the management of the national system is conducted by a board of directors appointed by the governor in council. This system of management has met with conspicuous success.
The capital structure of the Canadian National Railways has always presented a problem to the government of the day. In 1937 parliament dealt with this problem by enacting the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act. That act transferred to a corporation called the Canadian National Railways securities trust certain indebtedness of the national railways to His Majesty. This had the effect of eliminating from the balance sheet of the railways the amount of old loans for capital purposes and for deficits, together with accrued interest thereon, amounting to $1,218,642,195. Of this amount $270 million representing loans for capital purposes was transferred on the balance sheet to proprietors' equity as the value placed on the capital stock of the securities trust.
The capital revision act, however, did not deal with the large funded debt in the hands of the public and did not go further than I have indicated with respect to loans made by

the government to the national railways for capital purposes. In addition, the act of 1937 did not establish any policy for future financing of the railways except to proceed along the well-worn path of borrowing either from the public or the government as the need arose. In 1948 the government directed the royal commission on transportation to review the capital structure of the Canadian National Railway Company and report on the advisability or otherwise of establishing and maintaining the fixed charges of that company on a basis comparable to other major railways in North America. The recommendations of the royal commission on the recapitalization of the national system are found in chapter 6, pages 196 to 198, of the report. I propose to deal briefly with the recommendations of the commission and the corresponding provisions of the bill.
1.	Conversion of a portion of Canadian National Railways' debt into income debentures, recommendations 2 and 5 of the royal commission. The royal commission recommended that the fixed interest-bearing government loans outstanding on December 31, 1949, totalling $743,661,000 be converted into 3 per cent income debentures on which interest would be paid only if earned, and would not be cumulative. The government considered that it was undesirable to relate the amount of relief granted to the total amount of government loans outstanding at any given time. Such a course of action leads to the expectation that this type of loan could be written off at any time in the future that might appear to be expedient. It might also set an undesirable precedent in dealing with other crown corporations.
The bill on the other hand provides for writing off an amount of $736,385,405, being 50 per cent of the total indebtedness of the national company to the government and the public outstanding at December 31, 1951. In exchange for this release of indebtedness the national company will issue to the government an equivalent amount of 4 per cent non-cumulative preferred stock. In addition to this relief from excessive debt charges the bill provides for a ten year moratorium on interest due on $100 million of funded debt owing to the government.
2.	Newfoundland railway and steamship services, recommendation No. 1. The royal commission in its first recommendation considered that as a temporary measure the Canadian National Railways should be reimbursed annually by the government for the operating losses of the Newfoundland railway and steamship services and also for capital expenditures in respect thereof. Past experience indicates that segregation of
Canadian National Railways financial operations from the general accounts of the national railways is not desirable and that the railway management is in a better position to resist proposals for unnecessary or extravagant expenditures if funds are provided through the railway budget instead of being voted as a direct obligation of the government. For this and other reasons the government does not favour this recommendation of the royal commission. However, the government recognizes that the Sydney-Port aux Basques ferry is in a somewhat different position and the government proposes, although this is not included in the bill, to assume the operating deficits of that ferry service. This will be done by submitting to parliament each year an appropriation to cover the operating deficits of the ferry service similar to the procedure adopted by parliament in the case of the Prince Edward Island car ferry. In 1951 the deficit of the Sydney-Port aux Basques ferry was approximately one and a quarter million dollars.
3.	Reserve for something to come and go on, recommendations 4, 5 and 6. The royal commission recommended that after payment of interest due the public the Canadian National Railways be allowed to accumulate out of earnings in each year a reserve or something to come and go on, such reserve to be not more than the lesser of (a) one-third of the income after providing for all charges and deductions from income except interest on the company's obligations, or (b) the balance of the income after payment of interest on debts due to the public. It further recommended that to the extent that such reserves and surpluses had been accumulated losses, if and when realized, should be charged against such reserves and surpluses. It appears from this that the real objective the commission was seeking was the establishment of the principle that some portion of the annual capital expenditures of the railway for additions and betterments should be financed without adding to the fixed interest-bearing debt of the railway.
There are probably some additions and betterments required from year to year which do not add perceptibly to the earning power of the railway, and unless these can be financed in part at least out of earnings or by equity capital there will be a constant increase in the fixed interest-bearing debt of the railway and perhaps a continuing tendency for annual interest charges to rise beyond the railway's earning capacity. The bill provides for the annual purchase by the government during the period 1952 to 1960 inclusive of additional 4 per cent preferred stock in an amount equivalent to 3 per cent of the railway's gross revenues to provide

Canadian National Railways the company with a reserve to be used for ordinary additions and betterments. This percentage of gross revenue is a figure which would be subject to review at the end of that period in the light of circumstances existing at that time. Any capital requirements which could not be met out of this reserve and other reserves of the railway should be financed by interest-bearing loans either from the public or the government. These are matters in regard to which appropriate decisions can only be made at the time the financing is required.
4.	Securities trust; recommendation No. 3. The royal commission recommended that the shares of the Canadian National Railways securities trust now held by the government be turned over to the Canadian National Railways in exchange for an equal number of the company's shares. The bill provides for this to be done and for the continuance of the securities trust for the purpose of protecting the priority of government claims in respect of collateral securities.
5.	Future financing; recommendation No. 7. The royal commission recommended that any capital required to finance the company, in addition to reserves accumulated from operations, be obtained from the sale of bonds to the public and income debentures to the government. The government felt that this recommendation should not be adopted, not only because it implied that the national railways were to remain in a state of semibankruptcy but also because of the very serious consequences such a principle, once accepted ini respect of the national railways, would have in relation to the future financing of other crown corporations.
6.	Surplus earnings and deficits; recommendation No. 8. The royal commission recommended that surplus earnings, if any, after payment of interest on debts due to the public, the provision for reserves or something to come and go on, and the payment of interest on government loans be dealt with at the discretion of the directors. The bill provides that surplus earnings remaining after payment of interest on funded debt, income taxes and dividends on preferred stock shall be remitted annually to the government or the governor in council may direct that the whole or any part of the surplus remaining shall be applied toward the discharge of the obligations of the national system. If in any year railway earnings are not sufficient to cover all expenses, including payment of interest on funded debt, parliament will be asked to vote the deficit.
The government considers that the provisions of the bill provide a generous solution


to the problem of enabling the national railways to finance capital expenditures without an undue accumulation of fixed interestbearing debt and annual fixed charges. If these proposals are adopted the national railways would be relieved of fixed charges on government loans which amount to some $22 million, and in addition would have a moratorium for ten years on interest charges on another $100 million. The railways would also be relieved of the burden of the operating loss in respect of the Sydney-Port aux Basques ferry service. It should also be noted that the bill provides for a substantial amount of equity financing by the issuance of preferred stock which would be done even in years of poor earnings or no earnings at all, whereas the royal commission's formula would provide additions to the reserve only on the basis of a relationship to net income.
All things considered, I think the bill provides an acceptable solution to the problem of revising the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways.

Mr. Speaker, this bill is a rather complicated measure. For that reason, and also because it is to be referred for study to the special committee on government owned railways and shipping, my remarks this evening will be comparatively brief. On the whole, we believe this measure is a good one and that it will be of benefit to the men and women who are serving this country in their capacity as employees of our Canadian National Railways.
In the annual report of the railways for the year 1951 I notice this statement with regard to recapitalization:
The Canadian National has never failed to meet operating expenses, but except for the years 1926, 1928, and 1941-1945 has been unable to meet the heavy fixed interest charges with which the system has been faced since its inception in 1923. The royal commission-
Referring there, of course, to what is commonly known as the Turgeon commission.
-having studied the evidence presented in public hearings, reported:
Then there is a quotation from that report:
The Canadian National Railways has established
a case tor reduction of its fixed charges and for the desirability of the company being able to accumulate out of earnings a reserve or something to come and go on.
This recapitalization has been looked forward to for a good many years by those who are interested in our national railway. To me there seem to be two very important features about this measure. There is first of all the reduction of the fixed charges and, secondly, the desirability of the company being able to accumulate out of earnings a

reserve or something to come and go on. Those, of course, are the two points stressed by the president in his annual report.
Dealing in the first place with the fixed charges: in the annual report at page 33 we find that there is a very large debt held by the general public, amounting at the end of 1951 to $615,197,035, on which there was an annual amount of interest payable of $23,467,703. As I understand the bill, this debt to the public will not be affected at all. It will remain outstanding and will have to be met in due course by the railway. In addition to the debt owing to the public there was owing at the end of 1951 to the government of Canada, for loans of various kinds, a total of $857,573,774 on which there was an annual interest payment due of $23,347,412. This figure, of course, is after the reductions granted by the act of 1937.
In 1951, in order to meet these interest payments to the public and to the government, aggregating almost $47 million, the railway had available $31,783,119. That figure is to be found at page 26 of the annual report. It means that last year the railway was short $15,031,996 in the amount required to meet interest payments to the general public and also to the government.
The plan contained in this bill apparently is to take the total of these two debts, namely, the amount owing to the public and the amount owing to the government, and divide it in two. In that way we reach a figure of $736,385,405. That amount is to be taken away from the $857 million odd which is owing to the government, leaving a balance owing to the government of about $121 million, according to my calculations. In addition, of course, there will be $615 million odd owing to the general public. If I am wrong with respect to these figures I would ask the minister to correct me.
