Canadian National Railways This evening the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) has said that the government decided not to wipe out the total amount of the loans made by the government, in the belief that it was wiser to keep a certain amount hanging over the head of the railway. I doubt very much whether that was necessary. It does seem to me that when we were making this change it would have been better to follow the recommendation of the commission, and change all of this loan to the 4 per cent preferred stock. This would have given the railway just that much better start in its new day. After all, with this recapitalization the Canadian National Railways turns the page and begins with a clean sheet. I think perhaps it would have been wiser to change all of that debt, rather than leaving over $121 million still outstanding as a loan.
There is a second provision in this bill to the effect that on $100 million, which I suppose is $100 million of the $121 million to which I have just referred, there need be no interest paid for a period of 10 years, and no principal for a period of 20 years. During the second period of 10 years the amount of interest is left indefinite, with the figure to be set by the cabinet. It is difficult to understand the reason for this plan. There is no such recommendation in the report of the Turgeon commission, and the $100 million seems to have been an arbitrary amount pulled out of the air by the government.
When the resolution preceding this bill was under debate the minister rather led us to believe that one of the reasons this provision was made for the $100 million was the recommendation by the Turgeon commission that advances should be made annually for the losses incurred on the Newfoundland railway. However, he has cleared that point up tonight. I think it must be pointed out, however, that the Turgeon commission made very definite recommendations in favour of annual reimbursements to the Canadian National Railways for losses on the Newfoundland railway, and also for losses on what are called developmental lines. This reference will be found at page 198 of the report in these words:
It is also recommended that in the case of any developmental line which may hereafter be constructed or acquired by the government, in respect to which the capital expenditures required are large and losses in operation are likely to be incurred for some time, the entrustment of the said line to the Canadian National Railways be made on the same terms as are proposed herein in regard to the Newfoundland railway.
Those recommendations, if accepted, would have provided a means of helping Canadian National Railways in the years that lie ahead.

Canadian National Railways But instead of doing that, this measure just gives the right to waive interest on $100 million for a period of 10 years, and then allows the railway to pay a low rate for a further period of 10 years. It does not seem to meet the situation which was outlined by the Turgeon 'commission.
I wish to say a few words also concerning the second main feature, which is the accumulation out of earnings of a reserve, or what is described as something to come and go on. The Turgeon commission dealt with that feature at page >195 of the report, and apparently the suggestion was advanced by officers of the railway who appeared before the commission. This is what we find:
The Canadian National Railways has established a case for reduction of its fixed charges and for the desirability of the company being able to accumulate out of earnings a reserve for "something to come and go on."
On the following page the commission made very definite recommendations on how it might be possible for the railway to do that. In paragraph 4 of the recommendations we find the following:
That after payment in the first place of the interest charges on debts due to the public-
Your Honour will note that there is no reference here to debts due to the government, but merely to debts due to the public. -the Canadian National Railways be allowed to accumulate out of earnings in each year a reserve or "something to come and go on," such reserve to be not more than the lesser of-
Then there are two measuring standards.
(a)	one-third of the income after providing for all charges and deductions from income except interest on the company's obligations, or
(b)	the balance of the income after payment of interest on debts due the public.
Then there is a further recommendation contained in paragraph 5:
That after payment of the interest on the debts due to the public and the setting aside of the reserve or "something to come and go on" referred to in, (4) above, an amount equal to three per cent of the then outstanding government loans, or the balance of the earnings, whichever is the lesser, be paid to the government.
That recommendation had a psychological advantage. If it had been implemented in the legislation, then the railway officials would have been able to accumulate a reserve out of the earnings of the railway each year; and I think that would have been an attractive plan for them. As a matter of fact it seems to have been the plan which they proposed to the commission. But in section 6 of the bill we find that, instead of provision being made for the railway to accumulate a reserve out of earnings, the government for a period of nine years only, commencing with the present year, is going to pay to the


railway in each year three per cent of the gross earnings of the railway for that year.
In 1951 the gross earnings were something over $633 million. Had this measure been in effect last year, that would have meant the government would have paid to the railway about $19 million under this section 6. That money is to be paid into a special account and is to be Used for additions and betterments. In exchange the railway will give the government more four per cent preferred stock.
In such a plan there is, of course, in reality no provision for any reserve out of earnings. Instead of the earnings going, as the Turgeon commission recommended, first on the debt to the general public and then into a reserve we find that, under this bill, the earnings are to go first to pay interest on securities held by the public; second, to pay interest on indebtedness of the company to the government; third, to pay taxes under the Income Tax Act; and fourth, to pay dividends on these four per cent preferred shares. Then any earnings remaining over and above that will be paid to the Receiver General of Canada, with power given to the cabinet to apply any part of those earnings which remain over and above the first four items in discharge of such obligations of the national system as the cabinet prescribes.
I point out again that there is no provision for the railway to accumulate a reserve; and the provision for payment by the government is only for a period of nine years. I would ask the minister, when he closes the debate, to explain why that change is made from the definite recommendation of the commission.
Finally I think a word should be said about the difficulty of comparing the Canadian National Railway Company, which is a state-owned railway, with the privately-owned railways; and that is true both in respect of the Canadian Pacific Railway and in respect of class I United States lines. We are all tempted to think that by recapitalizing the Canadian National Railway Company we can place it in a position where it can be compared with these other companies and can be made subject to exactly the same considerations. But the Turgeon commission was careful to point out that such is not the case. For example, at page 194 of the report of the commission we find this statement:
What should be realized is that, while the Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway Company could and should compete in so far as operations and services are concerned, there are many ways in which the two systems are not comparable, and it is neither practical nor desirable to establish the capital structure and the fixed charges of the Canadian National system on a basis comparable with the privately-owned railway.

At the foot of page 199, setting out the differences, there is a further reference which reads in this way:
A realistic approach to the recapitalization of the Canadian National Railways must recognize: First, that it is not a privately-owned company and has, as such, advantages, e.g., exemption from income tax-
Of course that advantage will no longer apply, as I understand it.
-and relief from credit problems; second-
And here we have one of the great handicaps of the state-owned railway.
-that it must operate railways in the public interest regardless of whether or not they may be profitable; third, that its earnings are consequently harder to forecast than in the ordinary case; fourth, that considerations ordinarily applicable to private companies on a recapitalization do not apply to it with anything like the same force or effect.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) himself said something to the same effect during the debate on the resolution. I am referring to page 2908 of Hansard. At that page it will be found that I asked him a question as follows:
Is it the intention that this measure will put the Canadian National Railways in the position of being used as a yardstick for the setting of freight rates? At the present time I understand that the Canadian Pacific Railway is used as that yardstick. Will the result of this measure be that the Canadian National Railways will be used instead of the Canadian Pacific Railway as the yardstick for setting the rates?
To that question the minister replied as follows:
Well, in so far as I can ascertain, the Canadian Pacific Railway will remain the yardstick by which rates will be fixed under the jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners. This bill does not change that position. It would be for the board of transport commissioners to determine whether or not they want to use another yardstick. Whether they will or not, I am not in a position to say, but it is their responsibility.
The commission also dealt with that question. I read again from page 199 where they said:
In recent years Canadian National Railways' earnings have resulted from rates established on the basis of Canadian Pacific Railway's requirements. If this continues to be the case in the future, and if rates are established which will enable the Canadian Pacific Railway Company to earn its requirements as determined by the board of transport commissioners, it seems assured that on the average Canadian National Railways' earnings will be more than sufficient to pay interest on its debt to the public.
If the recommendations of the commission are carried out, and if good judgment and common sense are exercised in the future in the financing of improvements and betterments, there is no reason why the Canadian National Railways should again be burdened with excessive fixed charges.
As I said in opening, Mr. Speaker, the bill is to be reviewed by a committee, and it will be possible for that committee to call officials of the railway in order to get further
Canadian National Railways information concerning this measure. We hope it will be possible for the committee to make changes in the bill, should it be found that there are ways of improving it. We hope also that the bill will be of great benefit to the country at large, and that it will give encouragement to our railwaymen. They have been waiting for this measure. I have here a statement made by Mr. Donald Gordon, president of the Canadian National Railways, just last month when speaking in Toronto to the interdepartmental educational association, in which he summed up very neatly the hopes and the wishes of the company with regard to recapitalization. He is quoted as saying that he expected the C.N.R. recapitalization plan would be brought into operation in the near future, and then he went on to say:
This will clean the windows of our financial house. Once the legacy of excessive debt has been lifted from our shoulders, we will be judged entirely on our merits, and it will be a challenge to everyone in the organization to show what we can do.
We hope this bill will put Mr. Gordon and his fellow workers in that position, and we wish them all good luck as they start out under this new plan.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret to have to disagree with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), but my idea of the debate we have before us now is that we should give more importance to facts than to the report of the royal commission on transportation; and facts are there and they speak for themselves. If I am not allowed to read this extract from the bylaws of the Canadian-National Railways, public documents and part of the argument I am making now, I will' summarize them. I will do so by saying that in 1927 the deputy minister of railways and canals was a member of the executive committee of the Canadian National Railways which was empowered to exercise all powers which the directors were authorized to exercise. My contention, and I say that without offence to anyone and just because I believe in control of expenditure, is that it was a safeguard for -the government and for the country, as well as for Sir Henry Thornton and the management of the Canadian National Railways at that time. A representative of the government was there attending each sitting of the executive committee of the Canadian National Railways. It was a safeguard for everybody because I do not find it fair for the Minister of Transport, for the government itself and for all of us to be responsible for such tremendous expenditures when we cannot have any information about what is going on, and when we have reports that are beautifully illustrated, that may be very costly, but which mean nothing because when we ask for any information in detail

Canadian National Railways we are told that the matter should be dealt with before the committee adjourns, or things like that, as was said to me at a sitting which concluded at a quarter to seven at night. We are not at ease to scrutinize the expenditures made by the Canadian National Railways in order to protect the management just as well as to protect the government and to protect ourselves in this matter.
According to chapter 8 of the statutes of 1945 there was an amendment to the Canadian National Railways Capital Revision Act. I can summarize it as follows: The corporation is to be known as the Canadian National Railways securities trust, consisting of five trustees, the deputy minister of finance, the deputy minister of transport, the deputy minister of justice, and such two officers of the Canadian National Railways as may be named from time to time by resolution of the board of directors of the national railways. The trustees shall serve without remuneration. The same principle was applied by the act in 1945 as was applied by the bylaws voted by the directors to create the executive committee, of which the deputy minister of transport was a member ex officio.
Therefore, sir, I shall draw my conclusion. I had something else to say. You know, Mr. Speaker, we cannot deal just as easily as that with such huge figures. This $4,293 million in 25 years represents a yearly expenditure of approximately $172 million, and a daily expenditure of half a million. It is worth looking at it. When I think of the importance that members of parliament give to some picayune expenditure for wars or things like that, small things, they seem to be indifferent to a control being exercised by parliament-not by the government alone but by parliament-over that expenditure. I say that because I am convinced that the conclusion at which I have arrived is in line with the policy of the government at the time of Sir Henry Thornton, and which was followed afterward. The war changed it, but there is no reason not to apply it again for the welfare of the railway and for good government as well as the satisfaction of the Canadian people.
Very often we hear some members of parliament insinuating that everyone who is not a member of parliament shall be given a free rein, that everyone who has not been elected by the people is a genius or a wonder. It may be true, but we are responsible for what the genius and the wonder do. We have to render an account to our people. When we are asked a question about the management of the railway by any one of our constituents or anyone we meet on the street we say, "Well, they are great men; they


do not have to render account to parliament." They say, "How is that?" They would be shocked. They would not believe it. They would be astonished. What I cannot understand is the indifference of members of parliament with regard to the control that must be exercised on such huge expenditures, when they attach such importance to some minor details of administration. I do not say that in a way to criticize the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), because I have a profound admiration for him. I have known him for a long time. I know that he has a big department, and he is one of the hardest working ministers in the cabinet. He has a lot of responsibility, but let him be responsible only for the decisions he makes and let him not be responsible for the decisions that are made by others who are outside of the range of control of parliament.
I am not going to insist any more, Mr. Speaker, now that I have explained my case. I hope it is clearer than it was at the outset, when I had not completed my argument. I am very serious about it, and I have spoken about it to some of my friends down home and here. They said that it was pure common sense. How is it we cannot have these regulations for which I asked this afternoon? Time will tell, and I hope I shall get them so we can make a comparison with the past. I hope the government will not be shy in tabling these bylaws, because legislation was passed in 1945 which was precisely in accordance with the bylaws that were passed by the directors to transfer their powers to an executive committee of which the deputy minister of transport was a member. It is precisely because I have great confidence in the minister, and great confidence in his deputy, that I hope that in a short time the deputy minister of transport or anyone chosen by the minister will be a member of the executive committee of the Canadian National for the common good.

I shall be very brief, Mr. Speaker. If this matter goes to a committee, that is one reason for being brief. The other reason is that we have already discussed it at some length, and a third reason is that we are agreed on the principle of this measure. The only thing we are trying to do is make sure it carries out the purposes which are intended. We have already pointed out that we feel the operating officials of the Canadian National Railways should have some relief from the burden they are carrying. It may not be amiss, having regard to something that was said earlier in the evening, to say that even in the representations made by the Canadian Pacific Railway before the Turgeon commission there was a most generous reference to the operation

of the Canadian National. I shall read a sentence from page 185 of the commission report, and this refers to the representations of the Canadian Pacific:
It believes that the present management of Canadian National has achieved a high degree of efficiency in the operation of the railways committed to its charge. Any measures designed to provide an incentive to continued and increasing efficiency on the part of the Canadian National or any other railway are desirable.
That is true and we can accept it. On the other hand there is a question of being realistic about this matter, and of not taking off more of the burden than need be. The real question in my mind is this. This is the second major operation. There was a major operation in 1937, which I think we might all say was not a good year to make the change because we were still just struggling out of a depression. One looks at what was done then with respect, therefore; but now we have had a succession of what I think must be called good years. We come now to 1952, and I think it is very important that this second major operation, if possible, should do the job and that we should not have another hanging over us. It is with that thought in mind that I want to raise one or two points, though they may be gone into in more detail in the committee. The first thing I want to raise is a question which has already been raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra (Mr. Green). This being a subject which is quite uncontroversial, and a matter in which we are all aiming at the same thing, I am going to consider myself free, if necessary, even to differ a little bit from my colleague on details. We are all trying to get to the same point. There are various questions to which we are all trying to get the right answer.

I have here the statutes of 1950-51 and of 1950, and I just read the amounts appearing in the statutes passed for Canadian National Railways purposes. I am going to read the amounts for additions and betterments and also the net amounts for new equipment. First of all I read from the statutes of 1950: Additions and betterments, $30,872,000; new equipment, a total of $36,698,000 less $26 million which was financed separately, leaving a net of $10,698,000. That is roughly $40 million in that year. In the following year additions and betterments were $37 million; and in that year apparently the amount for new equipment-I have forgotten the exact reason-was considerably larger, namely $56 million. There may be figures that lessen that amount. Maybe I am not putting the problem quite accurately; but at any rate I am raising this point in connection with this figure of 3 per cent of the operating revenues which is the amount, under section 6, that apparently is considered necessary to give the railways, you might say, a working start. If actually that is not going to give them a start and if we are still going to have large amounts under the statutes year by year, then I again raise the question whether this operation is really doing the job.
I am not going to take more time tonight, Mr. Speaker; we shall have another chance to discuss this matter when we go into committee. I want to say again that, like every serious person who has looked at this matter,

Canadian National Railways I recognize the need for giving relief. much that I can usefully add to this debate at this time; but first I should like again to express my gratitude to those who have taken part in this debate for the constructive remarks they have made with reference to this not too easy to understand piece of legislation.

I was not dealing with my hon. friend's question; I was speaking generally. Then I thought I might take just a few minutes to deal with some of the points that were raised. I was saying that in this measure we have gone a great distance to grant to the Canadian National Railways relief from their fixed charges and to bring them to a position not on a parallel with that of class I railways of the United States or with that of the Canadian Pacific Railway, for that matter, but to bring tnem on a more comparable basis.
I do not think it was the intention of the royal commission, by the formula which they recommended, to put the Canadian National Railways forever and a day in the position that they would never again have deficits. Neither is that the intention of this formula. The intention of this formula is to lessen the charges, to give more incentive to railway management and railway employees, and to encourage the railway to earn greater gross revenues. If that can be done, then a position should be arrived at which would free
(Mr. Macdonnell (Greenwood).]

the Canadian National Railways from these large deficit operations. We are proceeding to cancel the $736 million of the total indebtedness of the company, and in exchange therefor we are taking the preferred stock. We have postponed the payment of interest on $100 million for a period of ten years and of that amount of principal for a period of twenty years. We have included, or will include, in the estimates of the Department of Transport an item to cover the deficit operation of the Port aux Basques-North Sydney ferry service. That is going some distance. But it is argued by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) that it is not going far enough. Why do we not wipe out the $100 million altogether? Well, the government considered both the formula of the royal commission and the formula of the interdepartmental committee, and decided in favour of the latter. I think the royal commission would not have brought down the recommendation which it did, so far as a reserve for something to come and go on is concerned, had the government at that time decided to charge the Canadian National Railways with the payment of income and corporation taxes. When the royal commission brought down its recommendation on the reserve for something to come and go on that decision had not been taken, and they were not aware of it. It was discussed, I believe, at the time the financial administration bill came down, wherein most crown companies are placed in the same position as the Canadian National Railways.
I have been asked to explain why the change was made from a reserve to the 3 per cent of gross revenues. Well, the answer to that is what I have said already concerning the income tax, and also what I said in my statement, that the real objective the royal commission was seeking was the establishment of a principle that some portion of the annual capital expenditures for additions and betterments should be financed without adding to the fixed interest-bearing debt of the railway. If you take 3 per cent of the gross revenue it amounts to $18 million or $19 million, on the figures of 1951. But to that you must also add another $16 million for depreciation which the railway writes off and has the use of during the course of the year. It runs you up to $35 million or $36 million.
Then there is also the question which the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) raised, that under the royal commission's recommendation the railway would have had incentive to earn a larger amount. Well, the position is even better now because

if I could establish, and unfortunately I cannot, a dollars and cents application of the royal commission's recommendations and those of the formula as included in the bill I think I could show that the position under this bill will be better for the Canadian National Railways in the long run than it would have been under the recommendations of the royal commission. Will there not be -and I submit with deference that there will-a greater incentive to increase the gross revenue of the Canadian National Railways so that the 3 per cent of gross revenues will be a larger figure to the railway for additions and betterments?
Then the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra seems to think there is no reserve here at all. If he looks at section 6 (3) of the bill he will find that there is provision for a special account, and it is labelled a special account; and in a sense that is a reserve.

Some statements were made by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) that unfortunately I cannot let go by without answer. My hon. friend said the total amount involved in this measure was $1,400 million by way of relief. That is not so. The amount under this bill, as I said earlier, is $736 million. That is cancelled, and payment of $100 million is postponed. There is no $1,400 million.
Then my hon. friend proceeds to make it up by quoting section 13, the latter part of which says that the amount on the books of the securities trust shall be $378,518,135.02.
Canadian National Railways That, as the house knows, is the amount which was established as the value of the capital stock of the Canadian National Railways securities trust away back in 1937, plus the amount that has been accumulated on it until this day. That is not being wiped out. That is just the value placed on the shares of the securities trust, and the amount which my hon. friend quoted under section 10, namely $396,518,135.02, is simply $18 million added to the amount under section 13 (3). Eighteen million dollars is the value of the one million shares of the Canadian National Railways, no par value. Therefore these two amounts which have been referred to are not being wiped out at all, nor being cancelled. They have nothing to do with the cancellation of the indebtedness.
My hon. friend says that it makes a grand total of $4,293 million of benefit which the Canadian National Railways have received. I am unable to agree with that, and I must say to him respectfully that under the 1937 capital revision act $1,218,642,195.27 was cancelled, and under this legislation the amounts I have mentioned.
May I take just one more moment to deal with the point raised by the hon. member for Greenwood. I do not think there will be any difference in so far as the accounts of the railways are concerned after this legislation goes into operation from what it was before, because prior to this act the government had in its hands about $780 million of securities through the Canadian National Railways securities trust and the Canadian government railways and the like. After this goes into effect it will have as equity capital $1,517,000,000. That is a little more than my hon. friend stated, but that will be simply because of the transfer of the $736 million which is being cancelled and for which shares of preferred stock of the Canadian National Railways are being taken in exchange, so that all of this the government had before as security either in the form of notes, loans or bonds from the Canadian National Railways. Therefore nothing is being changed, and from the point of view of the public accounts there will be no change in the active assets of the government. The only difference will be in the wording or in the phraseology that will appear opposite these active and non-active assets in the public accounts. I do not think I have anything more to add, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Chairman, I understand the minister has a long and involved statement to make, covering all the activities of his department. I hope he will now avail himself of this opportunity to make that statement.

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the kind invitation of my hon. friend. I have known that he was interested in mail couriers, and probably that is why he has insisted upon having this statement. Perhaps I should say that this is a matter in which the department has been interested for a long time. As a matter of fact we have been working on it since the beginning of the session. A special departmental committee has been formed in the hope that we may be able to give further study to the whole question.
Many hon. members on both sides of the house have asked for a special committee of the house to deal with this matter. I am sorry to say that, as a result of circumstances, it is impossible to have the committee set up at this session. I may say to my hon. friends, however, that I would welcome the setting up of such a committee, and I would hope that at the next session this whole matter may be placed before a committee of that kind for further study. We would welcome any suggestion which would help to give further direction in this matter.
A good start; keep it up.

So far the only way to let contracts is through tenders. By that method the contractor would make the selection. We have given thought to the principle of prevailing rates, and I suggest that is a matter worthy of some further study. It is possible that the best method would be found in a modification of both, embracing a combination of the principle of tenders and of prevailing rates. However, this would be for the members of the committee to decide.
[Mr. Chevrier.!

Then the Post Office Act passed last year placed power in the hands of the minister in respect of amounts up to $1,000. As a result he could make readjustments after one year of service. This too is a matter the special committee could consider. As a matter of fact the whole question will be given to the committee. Let me add that those of us in the department do not pretend to have a monopoly on wisdom, and would welcome any suggestions which would have the effect of bringing to the department an easier solution of these problems.

May I suggest that the minister have prepared an illuminated address of what he has just said to the effect that, as a minister, he does not claim a monopoly on wisdom in the House of Commons, and I would suggest that such address be circulated among the other eighteen members of the government.
A noble example.

I am sure it would have a salutary and stimulating effect, if it is not too late. I believe all hon. members will welcome the suggestion respecting the appointment of a committee to study the problems of rural mail couriers, problems that have engaged the attention of hon. members from rural parts of Canada over a number of years. Year after year the suggestion has been made that a special committee be established to study the problem. To tell the truth I never could see any valid reason why previous ministers have declined a study of that kind. I know they had what they thought were valid reasons for refusing, but the explanations they gave to the House of Commons never seemed to satisfy anyone. They seemed to have the idea that all wisdom was confined to the department.
The minister's statement this evening ought to clear the air in that respect. When the committee meets it will have the opportunity of hearing some of the couriers themselves give firsthand information about their problems. I am one who from time to time both publicly and privately has indicated the belief that the problems connected with rural mail couriers were about as difficult as any found in parliament. It has been my belief for some time that the proper way to handle the matter was to place it before a committee which would have authority to hear from all interested parties, including the patrons on the routes. I am hopeful that the committee to be set up will give careful and detailed study to the problems that have arisen.
While I am on my feet I would make one further appeal to the minister, who seems to be in an open-minded mood. I refer to a
Supply-Post Office
problem that particularly affects districts such as the one from which I come. In many parts of Canada today population changes have been rapid, and the complexion of certain areas has turned from rural to city or suburban. When I first entered the house we had a population in my constituency of approximately 28,000 people. The census will show that this population has doubled in numbers. In other words there are about 56,000 people in the county of Peel now, and a great portion of them are in the southern end of the constituency. That has brought about great problems with respect not only to rural mail service but also other services. Many people who have come from the large, concentrated and well-developed urban areas, particularly the cities, are anxious to have something at least approaching the kind of services they have been accustomed to all their lives. That has created problems of course for the municipalities and the county, and they have attempted to solve them as quickly as conditions would permit. I may say that the period of readjustment in most of these places has been fairly satisfactory.
However, so far as the mail courier system and the post office service is concerned, there has been a great deal of trouble in keeping abreast with changing conditions. I think I appreciate the problem of the Post Office Department because the changes have come about very rapidly and of course it has been difficult to adjust their organization overnight to take care of them. The necessity has developed for an intervening area of service between the strictly rural mail route where stops at rural mail boxes are a long way apart and it is necessary to travel a considerable distance in order to service them, and the actual postal letter delivery service to the door. Between those two services there is a very great and difficult area that has to be considered. I understand that in the United States they have attempted from time to time to bridge that gap by a sort of suburban delivery which is more or less a combination of rural mail service and postal delivery service.
I am not sure that it has worked satisfactorily in the areas in which it has been instituted, but I do think the Post Office Department should not wait for petitions from people who want to be served. So far as possible I believe the federal government should make periodic surveys of these rapidly changing areas with the hope that in some of them in any event the surveys will show the need for a postal delivery service such as is provided in the larger cities. I know the arguments that can be raised against that proposition. There is the question of the

Supply-Post Office
numbering of streets, the type of sidewalks and roadways and many other problems.
Nevertheless I do not think the Post Office Department can very well postpone the solution of the problem much longer, because in one section of my constituency that I know very well a rural mail courier coming up the centre road north of Port Credit toward Cooksville has to try to service at one stop literally a forest of posts with rural mail boxes on them. At one stage it was so bad that the safety of the area was endangered. If I may, I should like to pay a tribute to the Postmaster General and his staff with respect to a part of the area of south Peel. After recommendations made by organizations and myself as the federal member, the Post Office Department instituted a survey in the southern end of the county of Peel which takes in Port Credit and parts of Toronto township. I understand from a newspaper report that appeared in the press only last Thursday that those who made the survey have reported favourably with respect to a postal delivery service in that area. I want to point out to the Postmaster General that according to the news item it would appear that the survey was perhaps much more limited in its scope than we had hoped because the whole area that includes Port Credit, Lakeview and other parts of Toronto township is now to all intents and purposes a city.
I am hopeful the Postmaster General will see to it that that whole area of south Peel is given a postal delivery service as soon as it may be possible from a practical point of view. I am not making these criticisms in anything but a constructive way. I assure the minister that from personal knowledge of the circumstances and conditions of the area I know that a postal delivery service is very badly needed. If there is any delay it will cause inconvenience, which I think should be avoided if possible, to those who have come there in such large numbers to make their permanent homes in that most favoured part of Canada.

I might say to my hon. friend that as a matter of fact we do make surveys and endeavour to determine the best way to give service. I might add that he need not despair because in the estimates for 1952-53 we are giving active consideration to the establishment of a letter carrier delivery service in the following cities and towns during the fiscal year: Port Credit, Dakeview, Ontario, twelve letter carriers; Prince Rupert, B.C., six, Renfrew, Ontario, and so forth. Therefore the locality the hon. member has just mentioned is actually under study, and we are trying to solve the problems he has mentioned in the house.

Would the minister make some comment to the committee with respect to the anticipated revenues this year? I note that at page 371 there is a figure of estimated revenue for the past fiscal year. Can the minister give us the best estimate the department has been able to make of the anticipated revenue for the present fiscal year?
As far as I can see here, estimated revenues are $122,266,674.65, but all the returns are not at hand yet.
I can appreciate it is the best estimate the department is able to make at the moment.
Yes.
That appears to indicate an anticipated increase of about $18 million over the revenue for the fiscal year 1951-52.

Excuse me; I might make a short statement on that. The operations for the fiscal year 1951-52 just closed resulted in a continued expansion of the service both as regards volume and revenue. The revenues were helped by the increased postage rates which went into effect during last year. The increase in rates helped to meet the increased costs of transportation and increased salaries to employees. The revenue for the past fiscal year reached a total of $122,260,000. Expenditures were also higher, amounting to almost $115,630,000, thus indicating a "paper" surplus on the year's operation of $6,630,000. On a basis of commercial accounting, that is taking credit for services rendered such as franking, savings bank, etc., and charging ourselves with the cost of buildings provided by the Department of Public Works, and other such features, the surplus on the year's operation would be approximately $1,250,000.
From this it will be seen that the Post Office Department is operating within its revenues, which is our aim and object, and turning back into service any surplus we make from time to time.
